# Spec-Driven Development — Evaluation

**Question from the sponsor:** Is spec-driven development (SDD) the right foundation for an agentic pipeline? Adopt only if it demonstrably improves execution speed, quality, traceability, and agent coordination — not because it's popular.

**Verdict: adopt a lightweight spec-driven core, reject heavyweight ceremony.** One spec document per non-trivial feature, generated by an agent, approved by a human, used as the contract between every downstream pipeline stage. Nothing more.

*Validated against 2025–26 industry sources on 2026-08-06 — the verdict held and sharpened; see §Evidence below and [validation-2026-08.md](validation-2026-08.md) §Track 1 for full citations.*

## Why specs earn their place in an *agentic* pipeline specifically

The economics of specs are different for agents than for humans, and that difference is the whole argument:

1. **Agents coordinate through artifacts, not conversations.** Human teams absorb requirements through standups, Slack, and hallway context. Agents have none of that — each pipeline stage starts from whatever is written down. Without a spec, every agent re-derives intent from the raw requirement and they drift from each other. The spec is the shared memory that makes an orchestrator-of-specialists design work at all. This is a *coordination mechanism*, not documentation.

2. **Specs convert rework into review.** The most expensive agent failure mode is confidently building the wrong thing: tokens burned, human time burned reviewing wrong code, more tokens burned redoing it. A spec moves the human judgment to the cheapest possible point — a 5-minute read of a one-page document *before* implementation, instead of a 40-minute review of a wrong PR *after*. This directly serves priority #1 (speed): pipelines that rework less finish faster.

3. **Traceability falls out for free.** Spec → task IDs → branch names → PR description all link back. When a production issue appears, the chain "which requirement caused this code" is a grep, not an archaeology project. This is also what makes the autonomy metrics in [../05-metrics.md](../05-metrics.md) measurable.

4. **Specs enable cheap-model routing.** A well-specified, tightly-scoped task is exactly what budget models (Kimi, DeepSeek) handle well; an ambiguous requirement is exactly what they handle badly. The spec stage is what makes the cost-optimization strategy in [model-routing-strategy.md](model-routing-strategy.md) safe. Without specs, everything needs a premium model because everything requires judgment.

## Where SDD claims are overblown — and what we reject

Honesty requires listing the failure modes, because they're real:

- **Spec ceremony can cost more than it saves on small changes.** A typo fix or config bump does not need a spec. *Mitigation: size threshold (below).*
- **Specs go stale.** If the spec isn't updated when implementation reveals a better approach, it becomes actively misleading. *Mitigation: the developer agent must update the spec in the same PR when implementation diverges; the reviewer agent checks spec–code consistency as a gate.*
- **Multi-document waterfalls (PRD + TRD + design doc + test plan per feature) recreate 2005-era process with AI theater on top.* Rejected outright. One document.
- **Spec quality is bounded by requirement quality.** Garbage requirement in, plausible-looking garbage spec out — and a human approver anchors on the plausible text. *Mitigation: the requirements-analyst agent is prompted to surface open questions and assumptions prominently at the top of every spec, so the human reviews the doubts first, not just the plan.*

## The adopted policy

| Change size | Process |
|---|---|
| Trivial (typo, config, dependency bump, one-liner) | No spec. Direct task → PR. |
| Small but behavioral (bug fix, minor enhancement) | Micro-spec: the task file itself carries a 3-line intent/approach/test note. |
| Feature or anything cross-cutting | Full one-page spec in `specs/`, human-approved before implementation starts. |

Spec format is fixed by [../../specs/spec-template.md](../../specs/spec-template.md): problem, scope in/out, acceptance criteria (testable), open questions/assumptions, task breakdown hook. One page is the target; two is the ceiling.

## Evidence from the field (validated 2026-08)

What current practitioner evidence says — full sources in [validation-2026-08.md](validation-2026-08.md):

- **The size threshold is the most-replicated finding.** Nearform's failure retrospective names "overusing SDD on minor tasks" a top failure mode; Hidde de Smet's three-lane model (Full/Light/No spec, light = one-pager) matches our policy almost exactly.
- **Heavyweight SDD measurably fails.** Eberhardt (Scott Logic) measured GitHub Spec Kit at ~10× slower than iterative development on a real feature (2,577 lines of markdown for 689 lines of code); Böckeler (Thoughtworks) reached the same conclusion testing Kiro and Spec Kit. The tool market is voting the same way — OpenSpec's whole pitch is "lighter than Spec Kit," and BMAD retreated from its PRD waterfall.
- **Honesty caveat: there is no published controlled data** showing spec-first reduces agent rework. The supporting evidence is consistent but qualitative (first-hand engineering write-ups + revealed preference in tool adoption); vendor numbers ("40-hour features in 8 hours") trace to no primary source. Our own metrics are the real test — which is why the validation plan below matters.
- **Terminology worth adopting** (Böckeler's taxonomy): ours is a *spec-first* flow (spec precedes code, then code is truth) — not *spec-anchored* (spec stays authoritative forever), which is where the staleness critique bites hardest. Our same-PR spec-update rule is the drift control.
- **Two policy additions from the research:**
  - *Exploration carve-out:* for emergent/agentic behavior, stakeholders can't articulate requirements until they see behavior — prototype first, spec after learning. Exploratory spikes are exempt from spec-first; the spec is written when the learning stabilizes into a feature.
  - *Cross-functional approval:* specs written and approved solely by engineers reproduce misalignment with extra ceremony. For user-facing or product-shaped features, the approver set should include product/design judgment, not just "a human."

## How we'll validate this (not just assert it)

The POC (Weeks 2–3) runs the pipeline spec-first. Week 5–6's repeatability run gives us a comparison point: we track **first-pass gate success rate** and **human-intervention count** per feature ([../05-metrics.md](../05-metrics.md)). If spec-first features don't show measurably fewer reworks than ad-hoc runs, we shrink the spec stage further. The policy above is a starting position held accountable by metrics, not a commitment.
